title: Theory of Mind and Emergent Coordination

questions.question: When teammates cannot communicate directly, what can observing one another's actions help them infer?
options: That the final result needs no verification
Which tasks peers may already be pursuing
Every peer's private prompt exactly
The environment's state with certainty
questions.explanation: An observed move can reveal a likely target, helping a teammate avoid duplicating work, but it is only evidence about intent. It cannot expose the peer’s private prompt exactly or guarantee the observer’s full picture of the environment.

questions.question: What belief does first-order Theory of Mind represent?
options: What one agent believes another agent believes
What every agent jointly agrees to do
What the environment currently contains without any agent model
What another agent believes about a fact
questions.explanation: First-order ToM represents one agent’s belief about a fact, such as “Alice believes X.” “Alice believes Bob believes X” adds a recursive level and is second-order, not first-order.

questions.question: In the Sally-Anne false-belief example, where will Sally look after Anne moves the marble while Sally is away?
options: In basket A, where Sally last believed it was
In both baskets because the story is ambiguous
In basket B, where the marble is now
In neither basket until another agent tells her
questions.explanation: Sally was away when Anne moved the marble, so Sally still believes it is in basket A and will search there. Basket B is the marble’s actual location; substituting reality for Sally’s belief misses the false-belief distinction.

questions.question: Which coordination metric asks whether agents perform complementary subtasks rather than duplicate one another?
options: Identity-linked differentiation
Higher-order synergy
Goal-directed complementarity
Raw task completion
questions.explanation: Goal-directed complementarity measures whether agents take different, mutually useful subtasks instead of duplicating effort. Identity-linked differentiation tracks stable roles, while synergy compares group performance against subsets.

questions.question: A multi-agent demo appears coordinated only when prompts say work together, and there is no control condition. What should a team measure?
options: Assume any successful run proves emergent coordination
Compare against a version without the coordination prompt
Count only how many agents were included
Increase the prompt's coordination language until results improve
questions.explanation: A no-coordination-prompt control tests whether measured coordination persists without instructions that directly request it. Assuming a successful run proves emergence leaves the prompt-dressing explanation untested.

questions.question: Long-horizon agents forget which belief belongs to which peer. Which design helps preserve that identity-belief binding?
options: Store other-agent beliefs in a structured external ToM state
Add more recursive belief levels to every prompt
Keep all beliefs in an unlabelled free-form transcript
Remove action history so the context is shorter
questions.explanation: An external ToM store keyed by agent identity keeps each attributed belief attached to the peer it concerns across long runs. An unlabelled transcript allows facts and owners to blur as context grows.
